title: The Regulator Calls
briefing: The Cold Chain Safety Authority is reviewing pharma distributors' governance. Valtren is in the first group. The lead supervisor, Imogen Raske, asks for a meeting with the Director of Risk and 'evidence that the board knows its risks'.

context.text: Valtren already has an open finding from the Authority's earlier inspection. Expect it to come up.
Your direct line to the committee chair is exactly what supervisors look for.
The whistleblower case is on the supervisor's file.

evidence.title: Supervisor's request
evidence.body: Board and committee minutes (12 months); the risk appetite statement; the enterprise risk profile; evidence of how appetite breaches were handled; any open regulatory findings and their status.

evidence.title: Your own gap check
evidence.body: Minutes before the committee redesign show little challenge. One open finding is two months overdue. The appetite statement and profile are current and well evidenced.

questions.prompt: What stance do you take with the supervisor?

options.label: Open and proactive: provide what is asked and point out the known gaps yourself, with the plan
options.feedback: Supervisors trust firms that find and tell them their own problems.

options.label: Provide exactly what is asked, promptly and accurately, and let the supervisor lead the review
options.feedback: Legally fine; supervisors will find the gaps and wonder why you didn't mention them.

options.label: Route all correspondence through external counsel to manage legal exposure
options.feedback: Signals you have something to hide.

questions.prompt: The open finding is two months overdue. What do you do before the meeting?

options.label: Close it if possible; if not, a board-approved revised date with the reason and interim controls
options.feedback: Shows governance working, even when late.

options.label: Leave it as it is: the finding is on track to close within the next quarter, which the supervisor will see
Explain which manager missed the date and what has been done about it
options.feedback: Accountability is the firm's, not one person's, in front of a regulator.

questions.prompt: How do you show 'the board knows its risks'?

options.label: Trace one enterprise risk end to end: profile, deep dive, challenge in the minutes, decisions, actions, KRIs
options.feedback: One clear trail beats a stack of documents.

options.label: Provide every board and committee paper from the year, indexed, so nothing can be said to be missing
A letter from the chair confirming the board's oversight of its principal risks

questions.prompt: Older minutes show little challenge. How do you address it?

options.label: Acknowledge it, show the redesign and recent minutes that record challenge, and offer an observation
options.feedback: Turns a weakness into evidence of improvement.

options.label: Ask the company secretary to expand the old minutes with the discussion that actually took place
options.feedback: Altering records for a regulator is a serious integrity breach.

options.label: Leave it: the minutes were approved at the time and the supervisor can judge them

questions.prompt: What longer-term stance should Valtren take with its regulator?

options.label: A regular, open relationship: periodic updates on the risk profile and major changes
options.feedback: Supervisory trust is a strategic asset for a pharma distributor.

options.label: Keep contact formal and limited to what the rules require
Work through the industry body to make the rules more proportionate for mid-sized distributors
options.feedback: Not a substitute for a credible relationship.

lesson: With regulators, credibility comes from openness: tell them your own gaps, show governance working with evidence, and never alter the record.
